strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge in unified multimodal models: adapting continuous CLIP-like encoders for high-fidelity reconstruction and generative tasks without suffering from semantic degradation or catastrophic forgetting.

The two-stage reconstruction training scheme with feature self-distillation is well-motivated and empirically verified, successfully maintaining multimodal understanding capabilities while achieving strong reconstruction quality (e.g., rFID 0.32 on ImageNet at 448x448).

Comprehensive evaluation across understanding (MMMU, MM-Vet, AI2D, MMVP), text-to-image generation (GenEval, WISE), and instruction-based image editing (ImgEdit-Bench), demonstrating competitive performance against comparable and larger models.
The ablation studies clearly isolate the contributions of the distillation loss and the dual-condition architecture (query tokens + last-layer multimodal states) for generation versus editing.
weaknesses: There are numerical inconsistencies between tables that require explanation: Table 8 reports UniLIP-1B with GenEval=0.86 and WISE=0.44, whereas Table 2 and Table 3 report 0.87 and 0.53 respectively.

Architectural and conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental, building heavily upon established frameworks such as MetaQuery and DC-AE, combined with standard feature distillation and multi-token conditioning.

The generation and editing training pipeline remains complex, requiring multiple decoupled stages (two stages for visual tokenizer training, followed by three progressive stages for connector and diffusion training).
Experiments are limited to a single scale (1B LLM base with SANA-0.6B DiT); evaluating scalability to 7B/8B LLMs would significantly strengthen the empirical claims.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental challenge in unified multimodal models: bridging the gap between high-level semantic representation in continuous CLIP-like encoders and low-level reconstruction fidelity needed for precise generative and editing tasks.

The two-stage reconstruction training with a self-distillation constraint effectively prevents catastrophic forgetting of understanding capabilities while injecting fine-grained spatial detail into CLIP features.

The proposed dual-condition architecture provides an intuitive and effective solution to the fixed-token information bottleneck in query-based MLLM-to-diffusion connectors, yielding strong performance on image editing tasks.

Comprehensive empirical evaluations across four distinct capabilities (multimodal understanding, image reconstruction, text-to-image generation, and image editing) show consistent advantages over comparable 1B-scale unified models.
Ablation experiments clearly validate each component, including the necessity of self-distillation and the complementary roles of query embeddings versus full multimodal hidden states.
weaknesses: There are notable discrepancies in reported numbers: Table 8 reports UniLIP-1B achieving 0.86 on GenEval and 0.44 on WISE, whereas Table 2 reports 0.87 on GenEval and Table 3 reports 0.53 on WISE. The authors need to clarify which checkpoints or configurations these values correspond to.

The core technical building blocks (feature self-distillation to mitigate distribution drift and multi-token conditioning for DiT) are largely familiar techniques, making the conceptual novelty somewhat incremental despite solid system execution.

The paper lacks comparisons against standard generative autoencoders (e.g., SD-VAE, vanilla DC-AE) in Table 4 to quantify the remaining reconstruction gap between adapted CLIP features and dedicated generative visual tokenizers.

Evaluation and scaling are confined to a 1B LLM (InternVL3-1B) and SANA-0.6B DiT; demonstrations on larger backbones (e.g., 7B/8B) or discussions on inference efficiency and sequence-length overhead when passing all multimodal embeddings to the diffusion model are absent.

strengths: Addresses an important and active research challenge in multimodal foundation models: unifying high-level semantic understanding with pixel-level generative and editing capabilities using continuous CLIP features.
The two-stage reconstruction adaptation with self-distillation effectively preserves semantic comprehension while allowing pixel-level reconstruction from continuous CLIP features.
The dual-condition mechanism sensibly identifies and remedies the token capacity bottleneck of fixed query embeddings in reference-based image editing.
Extensive quantitative evaluation across four distinct capabilities (multimodal understanding, reconstruction, text-to-image generation, and image editing) with competitive results at the 1B scale.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: The core techniques—combining autoencoder decoders with pre-trained vision backbones, applying an L2 feature distillation penalty to prevent catastrophic forgetting, and concatenating full token sequences with summary queries—are straightforward extensions of established practices in representation learning and multimodal generation (e.g., DC-AE, MetaQuery, BLIP3-o).

Insufficient analysis of computational complexity and scalability: In editing tasks, concatenating the entire last-layer multimodal embeddings with query tokens significantly increases the token length entering the connector and DiT cross-attention. The paper does not report the associated FLOPs, memory footprint, or inference latency trade-offs.

Restricted scale and scope: The approach is only evaluated on a single small backbone combination (InternViT/InternVL3-1B + SANA-0.6B). It remains unproven whether the distillation strategy and dual-condition connector remain robust or yield similar gains when scaled to larger models (e.g., 7B/8B MLLMs) or higher native resolutions.

Incomplete generation evaluation: Generation performance is primarily assessed via prompt-following benchmarks (GenEval and WISE). Standard image quality and distribution metrics (such as FID/IS on MS-COCO) and direct comparisons with the standalone diffusion backbone (unconditioned SANA) are absent, making it hard to gauge intrinsic visual synthesis quality.
Minor presentation flaws and typos (e.g., 'viusal' in Table 1 caption, and qualitative comparisons in Figure 6 lack visual side-by-side comparisons with prior baselines such as BAGEL or OmniGen2).

strengths: Clear motivation addressing a critical bottleneck in unified multimodal foundation models: adapting semantic encoders (CLIP/InternViT) to enable pixel-level reconstruction and editing without compromising understanding capabilities.

Comprehensive and strong empirical results across multiple multimodal tasks, including image reconstruction (Table 2), multimodal understanding (Table 3), text-to-image generation (Table 4), and instruction-guided editing (Table 5 & 12), outperforming several larger models with modest parameter counts (1B/3B).

Thorough ablations covering the multi-stage training recipe, self-distillation loss, encoder selection, and the dual-condition cross-attention design (combining both query embeddings and multimodal hidden states).
Detailed qualitative comparisons illustrating improved spatial alignment, detail preservation, and semantic adherence in generation and editing.
weaknesses: The core technical components are relatively incremental combinations of existing techniques: feature distillation to prevent forgetting during encoder fine-tuning, pairing with a pre-trained pixel decoder, and extending MetaQuery-style conditioning with hidden token concatenation.
The model operates under restricted visual resolutions (448x448) and a downsampling ratio of 28x/32x, which limits fine-grained text rendering and high-resolution visual generation.
Minor formatting and typesetting glitches in the appendix (e.g., stray prompt strings and text labels appearing in Figure 7 and Figure 12).

strengths: Clear, principled motivation addressing the fundamental conflict in unified multimodal models: enabling high-fidelity image reconstruction from continuous semantic representations (CLIP/InternViT) without catastrophic forgetting of multimodal understanding capabilities.

Effective two-stage training scheme combined with self-distillation loss, which cleanly stabilizes decoder alignment before gently adapting the vision encoder, preserving or even slightly improving perception benchmarks.

The proposed dual-condition architecture (leveraging both multimodal hidden states for detail retention and query embeddings for MLLM reasoning) effectively resolves the information bottleneck seen in prior query-based frameworks during image editing.

Strong and comprehensive empirical evaluation across all three domains: visual understanding (MME, MMBench, MMMU, AI2D, MMVP), image generation (GenEval, WISE), and image editing (ImgEdit, RISE), achieving state-of-the-art performance at compact model scales (1B and 3B).

Extensive and insightful ablation studies validating each individual design choice: two-stage vs. single-stage training, distillation loss types and loss weights, query length scaling, and component decoupling in the dual-condition setup.
weaknesses: Resolution and scale constraints: the model is currently evaluated at up to 448x448 resolution and 3B parameters, which limits performance on fine-grained text rendering and high-resolution generative synthesis compared to very large foundation models.
Minor formatting and typesetting overlaps in the appendix (e.g., text box overlays above captions in Figures 7 and 12).

The primary implementation relies on InternViT (from InternVL3) and SigLIP; while these belong to the contrastive visual-language pre-training family, empirical validation across classic OpenAI ViT-L/14 CLIP checkpoints would further substantiate the universality of the proposed adaptation.

strengths: Clear problem formulation: Adapting continuous CLIP representations for unified understanding, generation, and editing without discrete quantization or dual encoders addresses a well-recognized and challenging bottleneck in unified multimodal foundation models.

Sound and effective training recipe: The two-stage reconstruction strategy—pre-aligning the pixel decoder first, followed by fine-tuning CLIP with an explicit self-distillation objective and learning rate decay—effectively circumvents catastrophic forgetting while unlocking detailed pixel-level reconstruction.

Well-motivated dual-condition design: Combining learnable query embeddings (which capture high-level reasoning and knowledge) with multimodal hidden states (which preserve spatial reference details) effectively resolves the information bottleneck of fixed-query architectures in image editing.

Extensive empirical evaluation: The paper demonstrates strong results across four distinct tasks: visual reconstruction (ImageNet), multimodal comprehension (MME, MMMU, MM-Vet, AI2D, MMVP), image generation (GenEval, WISE), and instruction-guided editing (ImgEdit, RISE), consistently outperforming or matching larger unified baselines.

Thorough ablations: The manuscript includes detailed ablations on individual training stages, distillation loss types/weights, probe evaluations, query lengths, and encoder decoupling vs. unification.
weaknesses: Incremental architectural novelty: Many individual components (self-distillation for representation preservation, MetaQuery-style connector conditioning DiT, DC-AE decoders) are adaptations of existing methods; the primary contribution lies in the empirical integration and recipe rather than new conceptual paradigms.

Visual resolution and scale limits: The framework operates at a fixed resolution of 448x448 and is evaluated up to 3B parameters, which constrains complex scene generation and fine-grained text rendering compared to contemporary high-resolution generation pipelines.

Typesetting and layout artifacts: Several pages exhibit clear formatting glitches, such as overlapping text annotations above Figure 7 (page 17) and duplicate caption fragments directly below Table 20 on page 26, indicating hasty post-processing.

Lack of detail on feature distillation: The paper does not thoroughly discuss whether self-distillation is applied only at the final feature representation or across intermediate Transformer layers, nor does it analyze feature distribution geometry beyond basic L2/cosine distances.

strengths: Addresses an important and active challenge in unified multimodal models: resolving the tension between high-level semantic representation (CLIP) and low-level pixel reconstruction fidelity without requiring separate encoders or multi-stage generation pipelines.

The proposed adaptation strategy is conceptually straightforward and effective: a two-stage training scheme with self-distillation that successfully preserves multimodal understanding benchmarks while boosting image reconstruction fidelity.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning four distinct capabilities: image reconstruction, multimodal comprehension (e.g., MME, MMBench, MMMU, MMVP), text-to-image generation (GenEval, WISE), and instruction-guided image editing (ImgEdit-Bench). UniLIP outperforms several larger unified models (e.g., BAGEL, Janus-Pro, UniWorld-V1).
Thorough ablation studies analyzing each component: reconstruction distillation objectives and weights, the dual-condition formulation, encoder choices, and training stage contributions.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is relatively incremental, as combining self-distillation to prevent catastrophic forgetting in fine-tuning encoders and extending query-based DiT bridges (like MetaQuery and BLIP3-o) are established concepts in the literature.

Resolution and detail limits: The model operates at a fixed resolution of 448x448 with significant downsampling (28x/32x), which restricts performance on fine text rendering and fine-grained spatial details compared to modern high-resolution native generative architectures.

Drafting and layout artifacts: Several pages in the appendix (specifically pages 16 and 22) contain stray caption text and editing prompts inappropriately positioned in the layout, which detracts from overall presentation quality.

Clarity on the dual-condition connector: Section 3.2 and Figure 4 describe concatenating multimodal hidden states and query embeddings into a 6-layer LLM-like connector before DiT cross-attention; additional details regarding token lengths, computational overhead, and attention masking between condition tokens would improve reproducibility.

strengths: Clear motivation and well-executed unification: The paper addresses a fundamental bottleneck in unified multimodal foundation models—the trade-off between CLIP's semantic understanding and its lack of pixel-level detail for reconstruction/generation—without relying on lossy discretization or computationally heavy multi-stage diffusion decoders.

Effective training methodology: The two-stage reconstruction strategy combined with self-distillation constraints successfully prevents catastrophic forgetting in the visual encoder while endowing it with strong image reconstruction capabilities.

Dual-condition architecture design: Combining MLLM hidden states with learnable query embeddings effectively resolves the information bottleneck of fixed-token queries, directly translating to substantial gains in image editing fidelity and consistency.

Strong and comprehensive empirical evaluation: UniLIP (1B and 3B) achieves state-of-the-art results among unified models across reconstruction, multimodal understanding (retaining or even improving InternViT scores), text-to-image generation (GenEval, WISE), and instruction-based editing (ImgEdit), frequently outperforming much larger unified models (e.g., BAGEL 7B, UniWorld-V1 12B).

Thorough ablation studies and efficiency: The paper provides informative ablations dissecting each stage, distillation loss variations, condition types, and tokenizer choices, alongside convincing inference latency improvements over autoregressive and two-stage diffusion baselines.
weaknesses: Resolution and text rendering constraints: As acknowledged in the limitations, the framework is currently evaluated at 448x448 resolution, which constrains fine detail reproduction and complex text rendering compared to dedicated high-resolution diffusion models.

Architectural specificity: While Figure 4 outlines the dual-condition setup, the exact DiT cross-attention implementation (e.g., whether hidden states and query tokens are concatenated along the sequence dimension or routed via separate cross-attention/adaptive normalization layers) could be described with more architectural formality.

Formatting and overlay artifacts in Appendix: There are minor layout glitches where text strings are overlaid across figures in the appendix (e.g., prompt labels superimposed above Figure 6 on page 16 and above Figure 10 on page 22).

strengths: Clear motivation and problem framing: addresses the crucial trade-off between semantic understanding and high-fidelity pixel reconstruction in unified multimodal models by adapting continuous CLIP features rather than quantizing them or relying on complex two-stage diffusion pipelines.

Effective and well-validated training scheme: the two-stage reconstruction approach with self-distillation successfully prevents catastrophic forgetting in representation learning, preserving (and even marginally improving) downstream multimodal understanding performance while achieving low reconstruction error (rFID 0.31, PSNR 24.62).

Thoughtful dual-condition architecture: concatenating multimodal hidden states with learnable query embeddings effectively overcomes the information bottleneck of fixed-length queries during image editing tasks, preserving fine-grained reference details.

Strong and comprehensive empirical results: UniLIP achieves top-tier results on generation (GenEval, WISE) and editing (ImgEdit-Bench) benchmarks, consistently outperforming several substantially larger unified models (e.g., BAGEL 7B, UniWorld-V1 12B).
Thorough ablation studies analyzing the individual contribution of self-distillation loss, learning rate decay, dual conditions, tokenizer choices, and multi-stage training schedules.
weaknesses: Incremental conceptual novelty: the overall pipeline is largely an integration and fine-tuning recipe combining existing modules (InternViT, DC-AE decoder, SANA DiT, MetaQuery bridging) with standard MSE-based feature distillation and GAN training.

Formatting and rendering artifacts: there are noticeable typesetting glitches in the appendix figures (e.g., residual prompt text strings overlaying the loss curves in Figure 6 on page 16, and duplicated figure captions/labels beneath Figure 10 on page 22).

Limited evaluation scope for instruction-guided editing: editing evaluation is predominantly centered on ImgEdit-Bench; assessing the model on additional standard editing benchmarks (e.g., MagicBrush, InstructPix2Pix test sets) or user preference studies would provide a more complete assessment.

Resolution and aspect ratio constraints: the framework is currently evaluated at a fixed 448x448 resolution with a high downsampling ratio (32x/28x), without clear details or validation on handling dynamic aspect ratios or higher resolutions common in modern MLLMs.
